fixes.explanation: It's her beloved at the door, friend. She says, "A sound! My beloved is knocking…" (Song of Solomon 5:2). Then he speaks up himself: "Open to me, my sister, my darling, my dove, my flawless one." A knock at night, and he really wants in.

Open is it. He says, "Open to me…" and then tells her his head is drenched with dew and his hair with the dampness of the night (Song of Solomon 5:2). I think a man dripping like that wants that door open, and fast. I'd be knocking with my whole mustache.

I get why feet came to mind, since she did just wash hers in verse 3. But in verse 4 the pounding is her heart. "My beloved put his hand to the latch; my heart pounded for him." Her feet are in the song, but this verse is about her heart.
The text says the opposite. She says, "I rose up to open for my beloved." (Song of Solomon 5:5). Her robe question doesn't stop her. She rises and goes to open the door.

False is right. She says, "I rose up to open for my beloved." and then, "I opened for my beloved…" (Song of Solomon 5:5-6). She asked questions about her robe and her feet, but then she rose. Those questions didn't keep her from the door.

If only. The text says, "I opened for my beloved, but he had turned and gone." (Song of Solomon 5:6). The one she opened the door for is no longer there. Then she says, "My heart sank at his departure."

The text never puts him down the street. It says he "…had turned and gone." and she "…sought him but did not find him." (Song of Solomon 5:6). It doesn't say where he went. All we're told is that she looked and didn't find him.

The text says the opposite. She says, "I sought him but did not find him. I called, but he did not answer." (Song of Solomon 5:6). She calls out and no answer comes back. I think that quiet is the heaviest part of the verse.
Beautiful it is. They ask, "How is your beloved better than others, O most beautiful among women?" (Song of Solomon 5:9). They call her that again in 6:1. Same title, both times they speak to her.

She sure does. From verse 10 through 16 she describes him from his head down: purest gold, hair black as a raven, eyes like doves, lips like lilies. She doesn't give a short answer. She gives them the whole portrait.

The watchmen are the ones who beat her in verse 7, but the text never has her mention them to the daughters. She answers the question herself. "My beloved is dazzling and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand." (Song of Solomon 5:10), and that's only the start of her answer.

False is right. She starts at the top with "His head is purest gold…" (Song of Solomon 5:11). Then come his eyes, cheeks, lips, arms and body, and his legs in verse 15. She keeps going after that to his mouth in verse 16, so head first.
Seek, friend. The daughters of Jerusalem say, "We will seek him with you." (Song of Solomon 6:1). Earlier she "…sought him but did not find him." Now they offer to seek him with her.
Greeting him sounds polite, but that's not their offer. They say, "We will seek him with you." (Song of Solomon 6:1). Their words are an offer to seek him with her.

She does. "My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to pasture his flock in the gardens and to gather lilies." (Song of Solomon 6:2). Back in 5:6 she sought him and did not find him. Now she tells them where he has gone.

No waiting is mentioned anywhere. When they ask where he has gone, she says, "My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices…" (Song of Solomon 6:2). She tells them where he is. Nothing in her answer is about morning.
True. She says, "I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me…" (Song of Solomon 6:3). That comes after the empty doorway and her search. I think it's a strong thing to say after that.
